column1: Define current and its unit; what does a negative current mean?
column2: i = dq/dt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s ≈ 6.24×10^18 elementary charges per second). Negative means the flow is opposite to the chosen reference arrow.
Energy per unit charge between two points, v_AB = v_A − v_B = dw/dq, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). Always between two points; a node voltage is relative to the reference node.

column1: State the three conditions of the lumped matter discipline.
column2: (1) No changing magnetic flux links any loop outside the elements; (2) no net charge accumulates inside an element (or node); (3) signals change slowly compared with the time waves take to cross the circuit.

column1: Which lumped condition gives KCL, and which gives KVL?
column2: Nodes store no charge (condition 2) plus charge conservation give KCL. No changing flux outside elements (condition 1) plus Faraday's law make ∮E·dl = 0, giving KVL.

column1: Passive sign convention: statement and consequence.
column2: Reference the current INTO the + terminal; then p = vi is the power ABSORBED. Negative p means the element delivers power.

column1: Why does SPICE report a negative current for a battery that is discharging?
column2: SPICE uses the passive convention for sources too: current is positive into the + terminal. A delivering source pushes current out of its + terminal, so it reads negative, and its @V[p] is negative.

column1: State Tellegen's theorem and why it holds.
column2: Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches (passive convention). Write v_k as node-voltage differences (KVL) and regroup by node; each node's currents sum to zero (KCL). No element laws used, so it holds for any lumped circuit.

column1: Lumped rule of thumb for digital edges, and the delay of FR-4 stripline?
column2: Lumped if one-way delay t_d < t_r/6. FR-4 stripline (εr ≈ 4.6): about 7.15 ps/mm, so 1 ns edges allow about 23 mm.

column1: Is mAh energy? Convert 225 mAh at 3.0 V.
column2: No: mAh is charge (1 mAh = 3.6 C). Energy = charge × voltage: 0.225 Ah × 3.0 V = 0.675 Wh = 2430 J.

column1: Average current of a duty-cycled device?
column2: I_avg = Σ D_k I_k (duty cycle × current for each activity, plus the always-on sleep current). Battery life = capacity / I_avg. A huge current at a tiny duty cycle can be a small share.

column1: Why is average power not V_avg × I_avg?
column2: P_avg is the average of v(t)·i(t); it depends on when v and i are large together. Only at DC (or with one factor constant) does it equal the product of averages.

column1: Distribution loss for power P at voltage V through resistance R?
column2: I = P/V, so loss = P²R/V² and loss fraction = PR/V². Doubling V quarters the loss; for equal loss the copper area can shrink by the square of the voltage ratio.

column1: Efficiency of a chain of converters?
column2: η_total = η_1 × η_2 × … ; loss = P_out(1/η − 1). Example: 97% × 90% = 87.3%, so 1 kW out needs 1145.5 W in.

column1: How much current does a 1 kW chip draw at 0.8 V, and what path resistance keeps the drop under 2%?
column2: 1250 A; 2% of 0.8 V = 16 mV, so R ≤ 16 mV / 1250 A = 12.8 µΩ. Hence regulators sit next to, under or inside the package.
